entities.name: Hannibalianus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Flavius Hannibalianus, a nephew of Constantine the Great, briefly held the unique imperial title of *Rex Regum et Ponticarum Gentium* ('King of Kings and of the Pontic Peoples') within the Roman Empire from 335 to 337 CE. His rapid elevation and subsequent brutal elimination underscore the volatile dynastic politics of the Constantinian era and the complex strategies employed to secure the Roman East, particularly against the rising power of Sasanian Persia. His short-lived prominence offers a glimpse into a potential, yet ultimately unrealized, transformation of Roman imperial administration.

Hannibalianus was born around 315 CE, the son of Dalmatius the Censor, a half-brother of Constantius Chlorus and thus a paternal uncle to Constantine the Great. Constantine groomed him for high office, granting him the honorific *nobilissimus*. In 335 CE, a pivotal year for the Constantinian succession, Hannibalianus was married to Constantine's eldest daughter, Constantina, who was also the widow of the Caesar Hannibalianus. Simultaneously, he was elevated to the unprecedented rank of *Rex Regum et Ponticarum Gentium*, a title reminiscent of Persian royalty, suggesting an intended role as a client king over territories in Pontus, Cappadocia, and Lesser Armenia, with Caesarea (Cappadocia) as its likely capital. This arrangement was likely designed to create a buffer state on Rome's eastern frontier, possibly under the overall suzerainty of the Roman Empire, without fully integrating these regions into standard provincial administration.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Hannibalianus's brief elevation and subsequent murder highlight the brutal dynastic struggles within the Constantinian family, directly impacting the succession and the administration of the Roman East in the 4th century CE. His unique title represents a significant, albeit failed, imperial experiment in frontier management.
